title: Strong Entity
description: Distinguish independent identification from optional participation, map strong entities to complete SQL identities, and query members without inventing dependent facts.
notes:
## Strength refers to identification

A strong entity type has an identifying key that does not require an owner entity's identity to complete it. Student can be strong when its institutional or internal student identifier independently identifies each occurrence. Department can be strong when department_id supplies its own identity. The term strong concerns the identification structure, not the importance, size, or physical reality of the represented object.

A strong entity can still have relationships, foreign references, and domain rules. It need not stand alone in every business process. For example, the model may require each student to belong to a programme while student_id still identifies the student independently. Separate the question which attributes identify this occurrence from the question which relationships must it participate in.

## Participation is a different dimension

Mandatory participation can require a strong entity occurrence to be related to another occurrence. A student can require a programme assignment, or an instructor can require a department relationship. Those business conditions do not automatically make the student or instructor weak in the identification sense if its own complete key still supplies identity.

Optional participation can also be allowed. A Department occurrence may be recorded before any students or courses are assigned. That example illustrates a possible lifecycle, but emptiness of related collections is not by itself a universal definition of strength. Read the identifying rule and participation policy explicitly rather than inferring the entire model from the current presence or absence of child rows.

## Own identity need not mean one column

A strong entity's key can be composite if the identifying attributes belong to its own specified identity and do not depend on an owner for completion in the chosen conceptual model. The number of key columns is not the defining distinction between strong and weak. A single arbitrary column name also does not automatically establish a reliable identity without the appropriate guarantees.

Suppose an institutional design identifies a catalogue item by a documented code. That can serve as its own key under the stated scope and lifecycle. Another design can use an internal identifier. Candidate-key requirements still apply: the set must identify occurrences across allowed states and be minimal under the model. Labels such as strong do not replace uniqueness, missing-value, or scope reasoning.

## Compare identification with a weak entity

A conventional weak entity is identified using its owner's identity together with a local discriminator. A room within a building can be modeled this way when room numbers repeat across buildings and the model treats the building as its identifying owner. Building supplies the owner identity, and room_number distinguishes the owner's rooms. The complete room identity is not the local number alone.

The resulting relational Room table can still have a complete composite primary key. Weak does not mean an SQL table must lack any key or permit unidentified duplicates. Conversely, using a surrogate in a physical mapping does not automatically settle every conceptual classification; discuss the represented identities and retained owner-discriminator business rule rather than judging solely from a database column list.

## Diagram conventions need a named notation

In common Chen-style teaching diagrams, a strong entity set is shown by a single rectangle and key attributes are marked using the applicable convention. A weak entity and its identifying relationship use additional notation. Other ER notations present identities and relationships differently. Say which convention is being taught instead of presenting one shape as a universal requirement for every modeling tool.

A diagram is a conceptual aid. It does not prove that the implemented SQL primary key, required relationships, or authorization rules match the drawing. Trace the mapping and inspect actual definitions before claiming an engine enforces the intended model. The label strong should remain connected to a clear identifying rule rather than merely the thickness of a line on a screen.

## A simple relational mapping carries the key

A straightforward strong-entity mapping creates a relation whose attributes describe its occurrences and whose primary or candidate constraints implement the chosen identity. Department can map to department_id and department_name. The identifier needs a uniqueness and nonmissing guarantee. Different departments can share a descriptive name if the actual domain permits that, so do not impose name uniqueness solely for visual convenience.

```sql
CREATE TABLE departments (
  department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  department_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL
);
```

This definition implements a supplied integer identity. It does not generate identifiers by itself, prove that every department exists in the real institution, or authorize a caller to create one. It also does not declare student or course relationships. Those policies require their own definitions and evidence even though the simple entity has an independently enforceable primary identity.

## Preserve independent occurrences in reports

A report of every department should retain departments with no assigned courses when the model permits that state. Starting from Course and joining Department lists only represented course participation. Starting from Department with a preserving join can keep empty departments and count their related course facts as zero. These are different report populations over the same model.

Count a nonmissing course identity to avoid counting the preserved unmatched row as a real course. A department with three courses should appear once in a department-grain summary with course_count equal to three. The join can produce three intermediate combinations, but that multiplicity does not create three Department entities. Keep result grain separate from conceptual identity.

## Descriptive changes preserve the occurrence

A department can change its displayed name while keeping department_id and its identity. Related course facts can continue to refer to that same identifier under the actual mapping. Matching by the old name instead of the modeled identity can lose the relationship or accidentally connect another department sharing the label. Identity should guide relationships and targeted updates.

This stability does not mean primary values are impossible to change. A correction or migration can require an authorized identity transition with appropriate handling of references. It means a descriptive rename should not be confused with entity replacement. Review which values identify the occurrence and which merely describe its current properties before deciding how an operation affects the model.

## Test identity independently of participation

Use two department occurrences with the same name and different identifiers, plus one department with no courses. The definition should admit those states if the documented policy permits them. Then attempt an existing identifier with a different name and expect rejection. That challenges the actual identifying rule instead of relying on a redundant name difference to conceal a collision.

Required participation needs separate tests if it is implemented. A primary-key check alone cannot prove every department has a course or every student has an allowed programme. Likewise, a foreign-key check can validate an assigned parent without proving the entity lacks an independent key. Each rule should be verified at its own boundary rather than treating one passing fixture as a complete classification proof.

## Avoid physical and conceptual shortcuts

A table with an integer id is not automatically evidence of a correct strong-entity model. It might represent a relationship, an event occurrence, or an implementation record with additional business identity requirements. A table with several primary-key columns is not automatically weak either. Read what the facts mean and how their identities are established in the chosen conceptual model.

Similarly, an entity is not strong because it contains many rows or is accessed frequently. Strength is not a performance claim. Index costs, scalability, storage layout, and query speed depend on separate engineering choices and measurements. Keep modeling vocabulary precise so the explanation does not become an unsupported comparison of database products or physical implementations.

## Review the mapping with explicit assumptions

State the entity occurrence, its own identifying attributes, relevant domains, and participation constraints. Explain how the selected relational mapping preserves that identity and which related facts it can reference. Then include both populated and empty participation examples and targeted identity failures. Record the actual engine and fixture scope when running SQL demonstrations.

The exercises verify independent department identity and zero-inclusive reporting on isolated synthetic fixtures. They do not certify every ER mapping, native foreign-key transition, exact MySQL provider behaviour, or production authority. A clear strong-entity explanation keeps independent identification and relationship participation separate while showing how both can coexist in a useful model of campus facts.

questions.question_text: What defines a strong entity?
options: It participates in every relationship in the schema
Its complete conceptual identifying key does not require an owner entity’s identity for completion
It has at least ten attributes
It only has single-valued attributes
questions.explanation: Strength concerns identification; participation and other domain dependencies can still be mandatory.

questions.question_text: In the common Chen-style ER convention used here, how is a strong entity set drawn?
options: A double-line rectangle
A single-line rectangle
A diamond
A dashed oval
questions.explanation: Strong entities use a single-line rectangle; the double-line rectangle is reserved for weak entities.

questions.question_text: Department has an independent department_id key and can be recorded with no students or courses under the model. Which classification fits its identification?
options: A weak entity, because it needs students to be meaningful
A strong entity, because it can be uniquely identified by its own key regardless of related data
Neither strong nor weak
A derived entity
questions.explanation: The independent identifying key establishes strength. Zero current participation is compatible with the stated policy but is not the sole definition.

questions.question_text: True or false: a strong entity can never have mandatory (total) participation in a relationship.
options: True — strength and participation are the same property
False — strength (self-identification) and participation constraints are independent properties
True, but only for weak entities
False, but only in EER diagrams
questions.explanation: A strong entity can still be required to participate in a relationship; identifiability and participation are separate concepts.

questions.question_text: What is the key differentiator between a strong entity and a weak entity?
options: Strong entities have more attributes overall
A strong entity has its own full primary key; a weak entity does not and depends on an owner entity for full identification
Weak entities cannot have any attributes
Strong entities cannot participate in recursive relationships
questions.explanation: This is the core strong-vs-weak distinction: self-sufficient identification vs. dependence on an owner.

questions.question_text: Under a conventional identifying weak-entity mapping, how do the identity choices differ from a strong-entity mapping?
options: The strong type has an independent complete conceptual key; the weak mapping combines owner identity with a local discriminator
They are mapped identically
A strong entity never becomes a table
A weak entity's table has no foreign key at all
questions.explanation: The strong key can itself be composite. A weak mapped relation still has a complete combined identity under the conventional mapping.

questions.question_text: Which entity set in the college database is a clear example of a strong entity?
options: A Dependent that only exists via an Employee
Student, identified independently by Roll_No
A line item that only exists via an Order
None of the above
questions.explanation: Student has its own key (Roll_No) and does not need another entity set to be identified.

questions.question_text: Why is it incorrect to say 'strong entities never depend on other entities in any sense'?
options: Because strong entities can still be involved in mandatory relationships (existence/business dependency) while still having independent identification
Because all entities are technically weak
Because strong entities have no attributes
Because the term 'strong' refers only to physical storage strength
questions.explanation: 'Strong' refers strictly to self-sufficient identification (having a primary key), not to whether business rules require participation elsewhere.

questions.question_text: Does strong imply no mandatory relationships?
options: Yes; all strong entities must be isolated
No; independent identification and participation are separate
Only if names repeat
Only if ids are integers
questions.explanation: The model can require relationships without owner-dependent identity.

questions.question_text: Can a strong identifying key contain multiple attributes?
options: No; every composite key is weak
Only if none are unique
Yes; key width alone does not determine weakness
Only if stored without a primary constraint
questions.explanation: Identification dependence, not column count, is the distinction.

questions.question_text: What identifies a strong Department occurrence in the example?
options: The number of courses currently assigned
Its screen row position
Its guaranteed department_id
The largest enrollment count
questions.explanation: The key supplies identity independently of current participation.

questions.question_text: Does a weak relational mapping have to omit a primary key?
options: Yes; weak means unidentifiable SQL rows
Only if it has one row
Only if names are NULL
No; it can use a complete owner-plus-discriminator primary key
questions.explanation: Conceptual owner dependence does not prevent complete implemented identity.

questions.question_text: Why qualify the rectangle convention as Chen-style?
options: Other ER notations can depict the same concepts differently
Only one drawing tool can store entities
Shapes implement SQL constraints automatically
Rectangles prove production enforcement
questions.explanation: Notation and conceptual meaning are related but not identical.

questions.question_text: What happens when a department name changes under a stable identifier?
options: It must become a new entity automatically
It can remain the same department occurrence
Every course must change identity
The primary key disappears
questions.explanation: Descriptions can change without replacing identity.

questions.question_text: How should a report include departments with no courses?
options: Start from courses only with an inner join
Count every preserved row as one course
Preserve Department and count nonmissing course identities
Remove department ids from the projection
questions.explanation: The required parent population includes empty participation.

questions.question_text: Why can three joined course rows concern only one department entity?
options: Every joined row creates a department
Every course has the same primary key
Counts define entity strength
Join combinations differ from department identity grain
questions.explanation: The parent identifier still denotes one occurrence.

questions.question_text: What directly tests department identity enforcement?
options: An attempted existing department_id with a different descriptive name
A name sort
A programme lookup
Only a valid SELECT
questions.explanation: Changing descriptions must not make a duplicate identifier acceptable.

questions.question_text: Does a primary-key test establish required course participation?
options: Yes; primary keys count children
No; that is a separate modeled rule
Only if the table is empty
Only if the name is required
questions.explanation: Identity enforcement and participation enforcement differ.

questions.question_text: Why is an integer id column insufficient by itself to classify a model?
options: Integers cannot identify entities
Every integer is a foreign key
The relation may represent different kinds of facts and business identities
Every id defines a student
questions.explanation: Classification needs fact meaning and conceptual identification.

questions.question_text: What does entity strength say about query performance?
options: Strong entities are always faster
Weak entities cannot be indexed
Strong entities always fit in memory
Nothing by itself; performance requires separate evidence
questions.explanation: Modeling terminology is not a performance benchmark.

coding_problems.title: Implement an independent department identity
coding_problems.task: Add PRIMARY KEY(department_id) to departments and return department_id and department_name. No automatic value generation is present. Repeated department names are permitted.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Add the department primary identity, then return the departments.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE departments (department_id INT NULL, department_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
constraints: Initial identifiers are unique and nonmissing.
This relational example implements the stated independent identity; it does not classify every possible schema by column count.
edge_cases: An absent identifying value must fail.
hints: The identifying role is department_id, not name.
Keep one primary constraint on the intended identity.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
ALTER TABLE departments ADD PRIMARY KEY (department_id);
SELECT department_id, department_name FROM departments ORDER BY department_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The declaration enforces the modeled independent department identity without incorrectly requiring unique descriptive names.

coding_problems.title: Keep independently identified departments with no courses
coding_problems.task: Return every department_id and course_count. Include departments with no courses as zero. One department can have several course facts without becoming several department occurrences.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE departments (department_id INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, department_id INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1),(2),(3); INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10,1),(20,1),(30,2);
constraints: The model permits empty course participation.
All supplied course references match departments; temporary query mirrors do not verify native reference enforcement.
edge_cases: A department can have no child facts.
Several children share one parent identity.
hints: Start from departments and preserve unmatched parents.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT d.department_id, COUNT(c.course_id) AS course_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN courses c ON c.department_id = d.department_id GROUP BY d.department_id ORDER BY d.department_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The report keeps the independently identified parent population while counting related course occurrences at their separate grain.
